articles.title: NASA funds spherical 'Aerobots' that could explore the caves of Saturn's moon Titan
articles.excerpt: An early-stage grant is offering a look at spherical 'Aerobots' that could zoom around the caves of Titan, in a demo mission similar to Mars Ingenuity.
articles.body: Spherical "Aerobots" may one day swarm the caves of Titan — a moon of Saturn that NASA says is one of the most Earthlike in our solar system. Titan is covered in rivers, lakes and seas of hydrocarbons, like methane and ethane, as well as a strange "karst" terrain including underground sinkholes and caves . No rover could easily traverse this surface, but flying vehicles may have more success. So a new grant, under the early-stage NASA Innovative Advanced Concepts (NIAC) program, aims to create small, flying vehicles that could explore those caves.

articles.title: How Often Should I Post, and How Do I Choose Topics?
articles.excerpt: Someone sent me a message asking how often I post and how I decide what to write about. I started typing a reply, realized the reply was three paragraphs long, and realized that was the second most us…
articles.body: Someone sent me a message asking how often I post and how I decide what to write about. I started typing a reply, realized the reply was three paragraphs long, and realized that was the second most useful thing that had happened to me all week, the first being that they asked at all. So let me answer both halves properly. We'll do topics first, because it's the part people actually get stuck on, and it's the part with the good news. "I don't know what to write about" You do. You just think your ideas have to arrive dressed up and important, delivered by a choir, on a subject nobody has ever covered. They don't, and it hasn't. Here's the thing I wish someone had told me earlier: you shouldn't look far.

articles.title: Security questions every senior backend engineer should handle
articles.excerpt: You are not being interviewed as a security engineer. You are being checked for one habit: whether, while describing a system, you notice who could abuse it. Security questions rarely arrive labelled.…
articles.body: You are not being interviewed as a security engineer. You are being checked for one habit: whether, while describing a system, you notice who could abuse it. Security questions rarely arrive labelled. They show up as follow-ups inside an ordinary technical conversation, and the ones that matter come back to a single instinct: treating input as hostile and asking who this trusts and why. Authentication and authorisation are different questions Everyone can define the difference. The interesting part is that authentication bugs are rare and authorisation bugs are everywhere, because authentication is one well-tested code path and authorisation is a decision at every single endpoint. The specific failure worth naming is trusting an identifier from the client.

articles.title: Python’s := Operator Is Tiny… But Surprisingly Powerful
articles.excerpt: Ever seen this in Python? if (n := len("Hello")) > 3: print(n) That := is the Walrus Operator It lets you assign a value AND use it in the same expression. Instead of: name = input("Name: ") while nam…
articles.body: Ever seen this in Python? if ( n : = len ( " Hello " )) > 3 : print ( n ) That := is the Walrus Operator It lets you assign a value AND use it in the same expression . Instead of: name = input ( " Name: " ) while name : print ( name ) name = input ( " Name: " ) You can write: while ( name : = input ( " Name: " )): print ( name ) 🔥 Why use it? Cleaner loops Avoid repeated calculations Useful in if , while conditions Makes some code surprisingly compact ⚠️ But don't overuse it. Shorter code ≠ better code. Have you used Python’s Walrus Operator before?

articles.title: I published our agent-security benchmark, including the attacks we fail to catch
articles.excerpt: Every company building AI agent security publishes a detection rate. We were doing it. The problem is that none of these numbers are checkable. You see "99% detection" or "blocks 100% of prompt inject…
articles.body: Every company building AI agent security publishes a detection rate. We were doing it. The problem is that none of these numbers are checkable. You see "99% detection" or "blocks 100% of prompt injection," and there is no test set, no failure list, no methodology, nothing to run. You are asked to trust it. I don't think trust is the right thing to ask for in security. So I published our benchmark, with the parts that don't flatter us left in. It's here: https://github.com/AndrewSispoidis/contemporary-agent-attacks Here is what is in it. 497 attacks and 1,172 benign samples, 1,669 total, across 22 categories. The detection engine scores 99.8% on the attacks at a 0.09% false positive rate. The license is CC BY 4.0. The methodology and scoring code are in the repo.

articles.title: On this day in space! Aug. 16, 1963: Wingless M2-F1 completes 1st glide flight
articles.excerpt: On this day in space Aug. 16, 1963: NASA's M2-F1 aircraft prototype makes its first glide flight.
articles.body: On Aug. 16, 1963, NASA's M2-F1 aircraft prototype made its first glide flight. This wingless aircraft kind of looked like a flying bathtub. NASA made it to test a new concept called the lifting body, which was an unpowered glider that provided an alternative way to return piloted spacecraft to Earth. Instead of pummeling out of the sky in a ballistic reentry, the lifting body landed sort of like an airplane. For its first test flight, the M2-F1 was towed 5,200 feet into the air by a C-47 Skytrain and then released. Test pilot Milt Thompson was in the cockpit, and he brought the glider in for a smooth landing in California after a two-minute descent. On Aug. 16, 1963, NASA's M2-F1 aircraft prototype made its first glide flight.

articles.title: Stephen King's 103-Minute Sci-Fi Movie Masterpiece Has Officially Returned to Free Streaming
articles.excerpt: Before The Shawshank Redemption and Stand by Me, The Dead Zone proved Stephen King was more than horror.
articles.body: Mention the name "Stephen King" and most people immediately picture haunted hotels, killer clowns, possessed cars, and enough small-town nightmares to keep Maine's tourism board awake at night. More than 50 years after Carrie launched his career, King remains synonymous with horror. King's best stories, however, were never simply about monsters. They were about ordinary people forced to answer impossible questions. What would you do if your child had terrifying supernatural powers ( Firestarter )? Would you knowingly send an innocent man to his death ( The Green Mile )? Would you rewrite history if it meant sacrificing the life you'd built ( 11.22.63 )? Horror was never the destination, it was the mechanism that forced his characters into impossible moral choices.

articles.title: Vulnerability giving attackers full control of Macs is under active exploitation
articles.excerpt: Screen-sharing bug lets remote hackers log in without a password.
articles.body: Dutch officials have warned that a high-severity macOS vulnerability that allows attackers to execute malicious code is under active exploitation. “The NCSC has received a notification indicating that active abuse of this vulnerability has been observed on multiple systems on which port 5900 was accessible from the Internet,” the Netherlands National Cyber Security Centrum warned earlier this week. “In all these cases, root had been accessed on the affected system and a Monero crypto miner had been placed.” Do you know if your screen sharing is on? The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-65400, received a patch from Apple last week for macOS Tahoe , Sequoia , and Sonoma .
